title: Move Pieces to Obtain a String
statement:
The strings `start` and `target` have the same length and use only `'L'`, `'R'` and `'_'`. Each `'L'` or `'R'` is a piece and each `'_'` is an empty cell. In one move you may slide a single piece by one cell into an empty neighbour, but an `'L'` piece may only step left and an `'R'` piece may only step right.

Starting from `start` and making as many moves as you like (possibly none), decide whether you can end up with exactly `target`. Return `true` if so and `false` if not.
constraints: start and target contain only 'L', 'R' and '_'
notes:
## Intuition

A piece can never jump over another piece, so the sequence of pieces read left to right (ignoring blanks) never changes. That means the k-th piece of `start` must become the k-th piece of `target`, and the two must have the same letter. Beyond that, an `'L'` can only end at or left of where it began, and an `'R'` only at or right of it. These conditions are also enough: each piece can be slid to its spot one at a time without blocking the others.

A brute force would explore every reachable board with a search, which is exponential in the number of pieces.

## Approach

1. Keep a pointer `i` into `start` and `j` into `target`.
2. Skip blanks with both pointers so each one rests on its next piece.
3. If either pointer ran off the end, the answer is `true` only when both did (same number of pieces).
4. The two pieces must have the same letter.
5. An `'L'` fails if its target index `j` is right of `i`; an `'R'` fails if `j` is left of `i`.
6. Step both pointers past this pair and repeat.

## Example 1, step by step

`start = "_L__R__R_"`, `target = "L______RR"`. First pair: `i = 1`, `j = 0`, both `'L'`, and `0 <= 1`, fine. Next: `i = 4`, `j = 7`, both `'R'`, and `7 >= 4`, fine. Next: `i = 7`, `j = 8`, both `'R'`, fine. Then both pointers skip to `9`, the end, together, so the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each pointer moves forward at most n times.
- Space: O(1): just two indices.

## Pitfalls

- Comparing only piece counts or only the order is not enough; the direction rule is what makes Example 3 `false`.
- Equal positions are allowed for both letters (a piece that does not move).
- When one string runs out of pieces first, the other may still hold one, which must give `false`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of both strings |
| `i` | index of the current piece in `start` |
| `j` | index of the matching piece in `target` |

narration.6: Keep pairing pieces until both strings are used up.
narration.7: Slide i past blanks to the next piece of start.
narration.10: Slide j past blanks to the next piece of target.
narration.13: One of the strings has no pieces left...
narration.14: ...which is fine only if the other one has none left either.
narration.16: Pieces cannot pass each other, so the k-th pieces must be the same letter.
narration.19: An L can only move left, so it cannot end to the right of where it starts.
narration.22: An R can only move right, so it cannot end to the left of where it starts.
